subject: Career
title: Why Office Politics Exists
description: One-minute skill: Why Office Politics Exists.

hook.text: 'I hate office politics.' Everyone says it. But politics exists wherever humans share limited resources.

buildup.text: Budgets, promotions, headcount, and attention are all scarce. Competing for them is politics.

discovery.text: Jeffrey Pfeffer's research at Stanford shows: ignoring politics doesn't make them go away. It makes you lose.

twist.text: The most politically skilled people often claim to hate politics. Their skill is making influence look natural.

climax.text: Politics isn't inherently dirty. It's how groups make decisions when rational analysis alone can't.

punchline.text: You can hate the game. But you can't opt out of it.

quiz.question: Why does office politics exist according to Jeffrey Pfeffer?
options: Scarce resources create competition that rational analysis alone can't resolve

details.summary: Office politics emerges wherever finite resources, competing interests, and human psychology intersect. It is not a dysfunction but an inevitable feature of organizations where people pursue differing goals within shared structures.
details.whyItMatters: Dismissing politics as corruption means ignoring the informal power structures that actually drive decisions. Understanding politics is essential for navigating any organization effectively.
takeaways: Politics arises from resource scarcity and competing ambitions
Every organization has both formal and informal power structures
Ignoring politics does not make you apolitical; it makes you uninformed

faq.question: Is it possible to have a workplace completely free of office politics?
faq.answer: No. As long as humans with different goals share resources, politics will exist. Even flat organizations and startups have political dynamics. The goal is not to eliminate politics but to engage with it ethically and effectively.

faq.question: Does office politics get worse as organizations grow larger?
faq.answer: Generally yes, because larger organizations have more layers of hierarchy, more competing interests, and more ambiguity in decision-making authority. However, strong cultures and transparent processes can moderate political intensity at any size.
